questions.question: A bank is called as Scheduled Bank when__________.

questions.explanation:

  • The list includes the State Bank of India and its subsidiaries (like State Bank of Travancore), all nationalized banks (Bank of Baroda, Bank of India etc), regional rural banks (RRBs), foreign banks (HSBC Holdings Plc, Citibank NA) and some co-operative banks.

questions.question: What is the main factor that differentiates Scheduled banks from Non-Scheduled banks in India?
options: Regulatory compliance with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
questions.explanation:
• Here, the correct answer is option ‘C’, that is Regulatory compliance with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)’.
  • Schedule banks are those banks that are included in the Second Schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, which means they are regulated by the RBI and fulfill certain criteria, including minimum paid-up capital and legal requirements.
  • In India, scheduled banks are those that are licensed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to operate as commercial banks and have the ability to deposit and withdraw money from the accounts of other banks.
  • Non-scheduled banks, on the other hand, do not have a license from the RBI to operate as commercial banks and can only accept deposits but cannot withdraw money from the accounts of other banks.
  • Another key difference between scheduled and non-scheduled banks is that scheduled banks are insured under the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation of India (DICGCI) while non-scheduled banks are not.

  • The minimum paid-up capital for LABs was Rs. 5 crore, with a promoter's contribution of at least Rs. 2 crore.
  • LABs are regulated by the RBI Act, 1934, the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and other relevant statutes.
  • They are required to be registered as a public limited company under the Companies Act, 1956.

questions.question: Small Finance Banks are required to maintain what percentage of their net bank credit as priority sector lending?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'C' that is '60%.
  • The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reduced the priority sector lending (PSL) requirement for small finance banks (SFBs) from 75% to 60% starting from the financial year 2025-26.
  • Under the new regulations, SFBs must allocate 40% of their Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) or Credit Equivalent of Off-Balance Sheet Exposures (CEOBE) to various sub-sectors under PSL.
  • The remaining 20% of the PSL requirement can be directed towards one or more sub-sectors where the SFB holds a competitive advantage.
  • The previous requirement of allocating 35% to specific sub-sectors has been revised to 20% as part of the new framework.

Additional Info:

  • At least 50% of its loan portfolio should constitute loans and advances of size up to Rs. 25 lakh in order to extend loans primarily to small borrowers.
  • The maximum loan size and investment limit exposure to single and group borrowers would be restricted to 10% and 15% respectively of its capital funds

About SFBs: 

  • Small Finance Banks are a category of banks in India designed primarily to further financial inclusion.
  • Their focus is serving the underserved and unserved segments: small business units, micro & small industries, marginal farmers, and other entities in the unorganised sector.

Regulatory & Legal Framework:

  • They are registered as public limited companies under the Companies Act.
  • They must obtain a license under Section 22(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. 
  • They are governed by the Banking Regulation Act, 1949; Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934; and other relevant banking, financial, and regulatory laws.

questions.question: What is the role of Sponsor Banks in the functioning of Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)?
questions.explanation:
• Here the correct answer is option ‘A’ that is Provide financial support.
  • Sponsor Banks provide financial support and guidance to RRBs, helping them in their operations.
  • They provide funding and technical support to RRBs, which are responsible for promoting economic development and providing financial services to rural areas.
  • Sponsor banks also help RRBs access capital markets and financial instruments, which can help them expand their operations and expand their loan portfolios.
  • By providing this support, Sponsor banks help RRBs play a more active role in the rural economy and accelerate economic growth.

questions.question: Which Union Territory (UT) among the following does not have Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is New Delhi

  • Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) are government owned scheduled commercial banks of India that operate at regional level in different states of India.
  • These banks are under the ownership of Ministry of Finance, Government of India, Sponsered Bank and concerned State Government in the ratio of 50:35:15 respectively.
  • They were created to serve rural areas with basic banking and financial services. However, RRBs also have urban branches.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct with respect to Regional Rural Banks?

I.Sarva Haryana Gramin Bank, a Regional Rural Bank of Haryana State sponsored by State bank of India.

II.Madhya Pradesh state  has  the highest number of RRB Branches.

III.Andhra Pragathi Grameena Bank , a Regional Rural Bank of Andhra Pradesh sponsored by Andhra Bank.
questions.explanation:
• Regional Rural Banks were established under the provisions of RRB Act 1976.
  • Regional Rural Banks are sponsored by any commercial bank, PSU or private bank.
  • Sarva Haryana Gramin Bank, a Regional Rural Bank of Haryana State sponsored by Punjab National Bank.
  • Madhya Pradesh state  has  the second highest number of RRB Branches followed by 19 RRBs.
  • Uttar Pradesh has the highest number of 36 RRBs.
  • Andhra Pragathi Grameena Bank , a Regional Rural Bank of Andhra Pradesh sponsored by Syndicate Bank.
  • Andhra Pragathi Grameena Bank is a Regional Rural Bank in India. It was established in 2006 as a Scheduled Commercial Bank as per Regional Rural Banks Act of 1976.

questions.question: Co-operative banks came into existence with the enactment of the Co-operative Credit Societies Act of ____________.
questions.explanation:
• Co-operative banks came into existence with the enactment of the Co-operative Credit Societies Act of 1904 which provided for the formation of co-operative credit societies.
  • To strengthen Cooperative banks, in 1999 a committee was formulated under Shri K Madhav Rao which came up with recommendations to preserve the cooperative character of such banks, lessen their financial risk, protect depositors’ interests, to align urban co-op banks with other banks in terms of prudence and norms.
  • A co-operative bank is member promoted and has to be registered with state- based Registrar of Co-operative Societies.

It functions with the rule of ‘one member one vote’ and ‘no profit, no loss basis’.

questions.question: Co-Operative Bank in India has how many systems?
questions.explanation:
• The 3-tier structure of co-operative banks includes :-a) State Cooperative Banks b) Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) c) District Central Cooperative Banks.

  • Co-operative banks have a 3-tier structure. Cooperative banks as a cooperative credit institution provide both medium-term as well as short-term loans.

  • Cooperatives provide Institutional credit which assists rural households involved in agricultural activities.

  • The government exclusively depended on development of cooperatives as an institutional source of rural credit till 1970.

questions.question: With which bank South Gujarat Local Area Bank Ltd was merged in 2004?
questions.explanation:
• LABs are non-scheduled banks function in the Indian banking space.
  • As at end-March 2009 there were only 4 LABs operating in India.
  • Local area banks are banks that are set up under the scheme announced by the government of India in 1996, for the establishment of new private banks of a local nature.
  • Unlike the RRBs which can operate in many districts with large number of banks, the local area banks can operate and open branches in maximum of three geographically contiguous districts.
  • LABs aid in the mobilization of funds of rural and semi urban districts. Six LABs were originally licensed, but the license of one of them was cancelled due to irregularities in operations, and the other was amalgamated with Bank of Baroda in 2004 due to its weak financial position.

questions.question:
What is/are common challenge faced by RRBs in rural banking?

  1. Asset quality concerns
  2. Inadequate capitalization
  3. Excessive profits
  4. Operational inefficiencies
  5. Surplus capital
questions.explanation:
Correct answer is Only 1, 2, & 4.

  • RRBs often face challenges related to asset quality, which can affect their financial performance and stability.
  • RRBs face several challenges, including inadequate capitalization, asset quality concerns, operational inefficiencies, and competition from other financial institutions.
  • Efforts are being made to address these challenges through reforms, recapitalization, and capacity-building initiatives.

questions.question: The first Regional Rural Banks named Prathama Grameen Bank was sponsored by ______.
questions.explanation:
• Syndicate Bank sponsored the first regional rural bank in India by name Prathama Bank, in Moradabad district, Uttar Pradesh on 2 October 1975.
  • RRBs were owned by the Central Government, the State Government and the Sponsor Bank (There were five commercial banks, Punjab National Bank, State Bank of India, Syndicate Bank, United Bank of India and United Commercial Bank, which sponsored the regional rural banks).

questions.question: Which regulatory body in India governs Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs)?
options: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).

  • The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the regulatory body in India that oversees and governs Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs). NBFCs are financial institutions that provide various financial services and products similar to banks but do not hold a banking licence. 
  • The RBI plays a crucial role in maintaining financial stability and protecting the interests of consumers in the NBFC sector.
  • As the governing authority, the RBI formulates and enforces regulations, guidelines, and prudential norms for NBFCs. 
  • It sets criteria for the establishment and operation of NBFCs, including minimum capital requirements, eligibility criteria, and business conduct standards. 
  • The RBI also ensures compliance with anti-money laundering and know-your-customer (KYC) regulations to prevent illicit activities and protect the financial system’s integrity.

questions.question: Recently, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has proposed a tighter regulatory framework for non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) by creating a __________ structure.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is four-tier.

  • The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has proposed a revised regulatory framework for NBFCs in a recent discussion paper.
  • The suggested framework involves a four-layered structure: Base Layer, Middle Layer, Upper Layer, and a potential Top Layer.
  • Base layer NBFCs would have their non-performing assets (NPAs) classified as overdue after 90 days instead of 180 days.
  • NBFCs in the lower layer would be referred to as NBFC-Base Layer (NBFC-BL).
  • NBFCs in the middle layer would be referred to as NBFC-Middle Layer (NBFC-ML).
  • NBFCs in the upper layer would be referred to as NBFC-Upper Layer (NBFC-UL) and would be subject to a new regulatory superstructure.
  • The top layer is intended to remain empty.
  • If an NBFC is designated as NBFC-UL, it would face enhanced regulatory requirements for a minimum of four years, regardless of whether it meets the parametric criteria in subsequent years.

questions.question: The classification of systemically important NBFCs is determined by:
options: The range of financial services offered
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Their asset size.

  • Systemically important Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) are classified based on their asset size.
  • This means that the determination of whether an NBFC is systemically important or not is primarily based on the total value of its assets. 
  • The classification of NBFCs as systemically important helps regulatory authorities, such as the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), identify and monitor NBFCs that have the potential to pose systemic risks to the financial sector.
  • Typically, larger NBFCs with significant asset sizes are considered systemically important because their activities and potential distress could have a broader impact on the financial system.

questions.question: What is the minimum Net Owned Funds (NOF) requirement for an NBFC to operate in India?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is ₹10 Crore.

  • The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) exercises its powers under specific sections of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011.
  • The RBI specifies that a net owned fund (NOF) of ₹10 crore rupees is required for certain categories of non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) to engage in the business of a non-banking financial institution.
  • The specified categories include Non-banking financial company - Investment and Credit Company (NBFC-ICC), Non-banking financial company - Micro Finance Institution (NBFC-MFI), and Non-banking financial company - Factor (NBFC-Factor).
  • Existing NBFCs falling within the mentioned categories, with a certificate of registration issued by the RBI as of October 22, 2021, and having a net owned fund below ten crore rupees, are required to achieve the NOF of ₹10 crores as per a defined glide path.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between NBFCs and banks regarding the issuance of demand drafts?
options: NBFCs can issue demand drafts but only for a limited amount.
NBFCs can issue demand drafts without any limitations.
NBFCs can issue demand drafts but only with the approval of RBI.
questions.explanation:
NBFCs cannot issue demand drafts.

  • The primary difference between NBFCs and banks regarding the issuance of demand drafts is that NBFCs are not authorised to issue demand drafts. 
  • Demand drafts are a form of payment instrument commonly used for transferring money from one location to another, and they are typically provided by banks.

questions.question: Which department of RBI is responsible for the regulation and supervision of NBFCs?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'B' that is 'Department of Non-Banking Supervision (DNBS)'.
  • The DNBS of the Reserve Bank of India is specifically entrusted with regulating and supervising NBFCs (Non-Banking Financial Companies) as per the RBI Act, 1934.
  • The regulation and supervision of NBFCs by DNBS is carried out under the provisions of Chapter III B, Chapter III C, and Chapter V of the RBI Act, 1934.
  • RBI supervises NBFCs through two methods: off-site (reviewing reports and returns submitted by NBFCs) and on-site (physical inspection of books and records).
  • The DNBS performs regulatory (rules, directions, prudential norms) and supervisory (monitoring, inspection) functions for NBFCs as per the RBI Act provisions.

questions.question: Under which section of the RBI Act, 1934, have Mortgage Guarantee Companies been notified as NBFCs?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'C' that is 'Section 45 I(f)(iii)'.
  • Mortgage Guarantee Companies are classified as NBFCs under Section 45 I(f)(iii) of the RBI Act, 1934, allowing RBI to regulate them under its NBFC framework.
  •  RBI issued a notification in 2006, bringing Mortgage Guarantee Companies under the regulatory framework of NBFCs, since they provide mortgage guarantee products (covering default risk on housing loans).

questions.question: NBFCs with an asset size of ₹500 crore or more (as per last audited balance sheet) are classified as:
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'B' that is 'Systemically Important NBFCs'.
  • NBFCs with an asset size of ₹500 crore or more are considered Systemically Important because their operations can impact the financial stability of the economy.
  • Systemically important NBFCs are those whose failure or operational issues could significantly impact the financial system and the economy at large.
  • They come under stricter RBI regulations (capital adequacy, exposure norms, governance, reporting, etc.).
  • The category is called:
    NBFC-ND-SI → Non-Deposit taking, Systemically Important NBFCs (if they don’t accept deposits).
    NBFC-D → Deposit-taking NBFCs are already systemically important, irrespective of size.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is true regarding the Deposit Insurance & Credit Guarantee Corporation of India (DICGC)?

A) DICGC Act was passed in 1961 to address bank failures in independent India.

B) DICGC is a subsidiary of the Ministry of Finance in India.

C) DICGC provides credit guarantee facilities exclusively for co-operative banks.

D) The maximum coverage amount under DICGC was increased to Rs. 5.00 lakhs in February 2020.
questions.explanation:
DICGC:

  • The DICGC Act of 1961 was enacted in response to bank failures in independent India, making statement A true.

  • DICGC is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), not the Ministry of Finance.

  • DICGC provides deposit insurance and credit guarantee services for commercial and co-operative banks, not exclusively for co-operative banks.

  • The maximum coverage amount under DICGC was increased to Rs. 5.00 lakhs in February 2020.

questions.question: SIDBI (Small Industries Development Bank of India) was established in ________ with the primary objective of promoting, financing, and developing small-scale industries (SSIs) in India.
options: 1921, Promoting large-scale industries and infrastructure projects
2001, Managing foreign exchange reserves for the Indian government
1990, Promoting, financing, and developing small-scale industries (SSIs)
1978, Providing microfinance to individual entrepreneurs in rural areas
questions.explanation:
Correct answer is 1990, Promoting, financing, and developing small-scale industries (SSIs).

  • SIDBI (Small Industries Development Bank of India) was established in 1990 with the primary objective of promoting, financing, and developing small-scale industries (SSIs) in India. It provides various financial services, including term loans, working capital finance, and project finance to SSIs.
  • SIDBI's focus is on fostering the growth of the small and medium enterprise (SME) sector, not on large-scale industries, MNCs, or foreign exchange management.

questions.question: Initially, the central government will own 100% shares of the NABFID which may subsequently be reduced up to____%.
questions.explanation: • Shares of NABFID may be held by: (i) central government, (ii) multilateral institutions, (iii) sovereign wealth funds, (iv) pension funds, (v) insurers, (vi) financial institutions, (vii) banks, and (viii) any other institution prescribed by the central government. Initially, the central government will own 100% shares of the institution which may subsequently be reduced up to 26%.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is true about DICGC?
options: It provides funds up to Rs 1 lakh to an account holder within 45 days
It provides funds up to Rs 3 lakh to an account holder within 60 days
It provides funds up to Rs 4 lakh to an account holder within 75 days
It provides funds up to Rs 5 lakh to an account holder within 90 days
questions.explanation: It will provide funds up to Rs 5 lakh to an account holder within 90 days in the event of a bank coming under the moratorium imposed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Earlier, account holders had to wait for years till the liquidation or restructuring of a distressed lender to get their deposits that are insured against default. The Rs 5-lakh deposit insurance cover was raised from Rs 1 lakh in 2020.

questions.question: The NHB was founded with the following goal:
options: Promote housing finance institutions as a primary agency.
Support local and regional housing finance organisations.
Provide monetary and other support necessary for such entities and for issues related to them.
questions.explanation:
• NHB has been established to achieve, inter alia, the following:

  • To promote a sound, healthy, viable and cost effective housing finance system to cater to all segments of the population and to integrate the housing finance system with the overall financial system.

  • To promote a network of dedicated housing finance institutions to adequately serve various regions and different income groups.

  • To augment resources for the sector and channelise them for housing.

  • To make housing credit more affordable.

  • To supervise the activities of housing finance companies based on supervisory power derived under the Act.

  • To encourage augmentation of supply of buildable land and also building materials for housing and to upgrade the housing stock in the country.

  • To encourage public agencies to emerge as facilitators and suppliers of serviced land, for housing.

questions.question: EXIM Bank was founded in which year?
questions.explanation:
Export-Import Bank was founded on 1Jan 1982 having the headquarter at Mumbai. It is owned by the Government of India. It also comes under Sec 45L and Sec 45N of RBI Act, 1934. 

EXIM Banks are special kind of financial institutions that provide wide range of financial assistance to the Exporters and Importers of a country.

questions.question: NABARD is wholly owned by which institution?
questions.explanation:
- NABARD is wholly owned by the Government of India.
- National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) is an apex regulatory body for the overall regulation of regional rural banks and apex cooperative banks in India.
- It is under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Finance, Government of India.
- The bank has been entrusted with "matters concerning policy, planning, and operations in the field of credit for agriculture and other economic activities in rural areas in India". NABARD is active in developing and implementing financial inclusion.

questions.question: NaBFID stands for ‘_____________’.
options: National Board of Financing Interior and Design
National Board for Finance Infrastructure and Development
National Bank for Fine, Interest and Development
National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development.

  • The National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development (NaBFID) is a specialized Development Finance Institution in India aimed at supporting the country's infrastructure sector, which can significantly gain from an enabling credit flow by means of attractive instruments and channelized investment.
  • NaBFID was set up in 2021, by an Act of the Parliament (The National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development Act, 2021), with the essential objectives of addressing the gaps in long-term non-recourse finance for infrastructure development, strengthening the development of bonds and derivatives markets in India, and sustainably boosting the country’s economy.

questions.question: Which of the following services is/are offer by EXIM Bank?
questions.explanation:
• Marketing advisory services – help Indian exporters in their globalization ventures by assisting in locating overseas distributors/partners, etc. Also, assists in identifying opportunities abroad for setting up plant projects or acquiring companies.

  • Research and analysis – conducts research in the field of international economics, trade and investment, country profiles to identify risks, etc.

  • Export advisory services – it offers information, advisory, and support services enabling exporters to evaluate international risks, exploit export opportunities and improve competitiveness.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct in the context of DICGC?
options: The deposit insurance scheme is compulsory for each bank and no bank can withdraw from it.
Each depositor in a bank is insured for a maximum of Rs. 5 lakhs for both the principal and interest amount held by him.
DICGC insures Commercial Banks, Cooperative Banks, but not Primary Cooperative Societies.
The premium for deposit insurance is borne entirely by the insured bank.
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'E' that is 'All are correct'.
  • All eligible banks, including commercial and cooperative banks, are mandatorily covered under the DICGC insurance scheme.
  • As per the latest amendment (effective from February 4, 2020), each depositor is insured up to ₹5 lakh, including both principal and interest, per bank.
  • DICGC covers Commercial Banks, Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, and eligible Cooperative Banks, but does not cover Primary Cooperative Credit Societies.
  • Banks pay the insurance premium to DICGC. Depositors are not charged any amount for this insurance.
  • Hence, all the given statements are correct. 

About DICGC:

  • Full Form: Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation
  • Established: 15 July 1978
  • Headquarters: Mumbai, Maharashtra
  • Wholly Owned Subsidiary of: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)

questions.question: How many regional and branch offices of SIDBI are in India?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is 5, 33.

  • The Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) is India’s top governing agency for licensing and managing micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs). It is administered by the Government of India’s Ministry of Finance. 
  • The SIDBI headquarters is in Lucknow along with 5 Regional Offices and 33 Branch Offices throughout the nation. 
  • Its mission is to extend refinance services to banks and commercial organizations, as well as invest in term lending and working capital loans to enterprises. 
  • SIDBI serves as the MSME sector’s primary banking institution.

questions.question: Loans granted by NABARD under RIDF are repaid in equal annual installments over _____ years from the date of withdrawal, including a grace period of 2 years.
questions.explanation:
• The RIDF, or Rural Infrastructure Development Fund, was created in 1995-96 by the government in NABARD, and there are 39 eligible activities approved by the government under RIDF. The main objective of RIDF is to provide loans to governments and state-owned corporations and enable them to complete ongoing rural infrastructure projects.

  • Interest rates payable to banks on deposits and loans disbursed by NABARD from RIDF have been linked to the then prevailing bank rate.

  • The loan is to be repaid in equal annual installments within 7 years from the date of return, including a grace period of 2 years.

questions.question: Which of the following is a function of NABFID?
options: Extending loans and advances for infrastructure projects.
Taking over or refinancing such existing loans
Attracting investment from private sector investors and institutional investors for infrastructure projects.
Organizing and facilitating foreign participation in infrastructure projects
questions.explanation:
• NBFID will have both financial as well as developmental objectives. Financial objectives will be to directly or indirectly lend, invest, or attract investments for infrastructure projects located entirely or partly in India.  The central government will prescribe the sectors to be covered under the infrastructure domain.  Developmental objectives include facilitating the development of the market for bonds, loans, and derivatives for infrastructure financing.
  • Functions of NABFID include:
  1. extending loans and advances for infrastructure projects,
  2. taking over or refinancing such existing loans,
  3. attracting investment from private sector investors and institutional investors for infrastructure projects,
  4. organizing and facilitating foreign participation in infrastructure projects,
  5. facilitating negotiations with various government authorities for dispute resolution in the field of infrastructure financing, and
  6. providing consultancy services in infrastructure financing.

questions.question: Under which act was the National Housing Bank (NHB) established?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer is National Housing Bank Act, 1987.

  • The National Housing Bank (NHB) was established under the National Housing Bank Act, 1987.
  • The NHB began operations on July 9, 1988, and serves as the apex financial institution for housing in India, focusing on promoting and regulating housing finance institutions and facilitating the development of a sound housing finance system.

questions.question: The Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) has been created under ____.
questions.explanation:
• In 1995-96, the Government of India had set up the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) for financing ongoing rural infrastructure projects.
  • The funds were released under RIDF are maintained by the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD)
  • The main objective of the fund is to provide loans to State Governments and State-owned corporations to enable them to complete ongoing rural infrastructure projects.
  • These funds are provided on a year-to-year basis by the Government of India
  • Under the RIDF scheme Rs. 51,283 crore have been sanctioned for 2,44,651 projects covering irrigation, rural roads, and bridges, health and education, soil conservation, water schemes, etc

questions.question: Which subsidiary of NABARD focuses on providing financial services to microfinance institutions?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'B' thata is 'NABARD Financial Services (NABFINS)'
  • NABFINS is a subsidiary of NABARD that specializes in providing financial services to microfinance institutions.
  • NABFINS Limited (NABFINS), is a Company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 and registered with Reserve Bank of India as an NBFC-MFI.
  • NABFINS’ approach to the business of microfinance is defined by its tagline “Balancing Business with Inclusion”. It adopts a unique model which leverages social collateral provided by the Self Help Groups (SHGs) & Joint Liability Groups (JLGs) by offering micro-credit at their doorstep, at the lowest interest rate among NBFC-MFIs to low income households, comprising predominantly women.

questions.question: SIDBI aims to facilitate and strengthen credit flow to ________.
questions.explanation:
• Mission: To facilitate and strengthen credit flow to MSMEs and address both financial and developmental gaps in the MSME ecosystem
  • Vision: To emerge as a single window for meeting the financial and developmental needs of the MSME sector to make it strong, vibrant and globally competitive, to position SIDBI Brand as the preferred and customer-friendly institution and for enhancement of shareholder wealth and highest corporate values through modern technology platform

questions.question: Under the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) scheme, what is the maximum amount insured per depositor for each bank?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer is ₹5 lakh.

  • The DICGC insures all bank deposits, such as savings, fixed, current, and recurring deposits, up to a maximum of ₹5 lakh per depositor for each bank. This limit was increased from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh in February 2020 to provide better protection to depositors.
  • The primary objective of the DICGC is to protect depositors' interests and promote public confidence in the banking system by ensuring that, in the event of a bank failure, depositors receive a portion of their funds back.
  • All commercial banks, including branches of foreign banks operating in India, Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), and cooperative banks, are covered under this insurance scheme.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements about NABARD is/are correct?

  1. NABARD was established in 1982 under an act of Parliament to provide credit facilities specifically for large-scale industries in rural areas.
  2. NABARD acts as a refinance agency for institutions providing investment and production credit.
  3. NABARD supervises and regulates cooperative banks and Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) in India.
  4. NABARD is solely responsible for the direct disbursement of loans to individual farmers.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer is 1, 2, and 3 only.

  • NABARD was established in 1982 under an act of Parliament to provide credit facilities specifically for large-scale industries in rural areas.
  • NABARD acts as a refinance agency for institutions providing investment and production credit.
  • NABARD supervises and regulates cooperative banks and Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) in India.
  • NABARD does not directly disburse loans to individual farmers; it works through other financial institutions.

questions.question: Which of the following is the apex regulatory body for the overall regulation and licensing of housing finance in India?
options: Ministry of Urban and Housing Affairs
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is National Housing Bank (NHB).

  • National Housing Bank (NHB), is the apex regulatory body for overall regulation and licensing of housing finance companies in India. 
  • It is under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Finance, Government of India. 
  • It was set up on 9 July 1988 under the National Housing Bank Act, 1987. 
  • NHB has been established with an objective to operate as a principal agency to promote housing finance institutions both at local and regional levels and to provide financial and other support incidental to such institutions and for matters connected therewith. 
  • The Finance Act, 2019 has amended the National Housing Bank Act, 1987. 
  • The amendment confers the powers of regulation of Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) to the Reserve Bank of India.

questions.question: The authorised capital of EXIM Bank has increased from Rs. 10,000 crores to _____ crores in 2019.
questions.explanation:
• The authorised capital of the EXIM Bank was Rs. 10,000 crores, which was increased to Rs. Rs. 20,000 crores by the Government in 2019.

  • The EXIM Bank started its operations in 1982, with the main aim of promoting foreign trade in the country. It provides financial and other assistance to importers and exporters of India.

  • The company is headquartered in Mumbai, and the current MD is Harsha Bangari.

questions.question: NABARD was set up with an initial capital of Rs. 100 crore contributed equally by the Government of India and the ______.
questions.explanation:
• NABARD was set up in 1982 on the recommendations of the B. Sivaraman committee, with an initial capital of Rs. 100 crore contributed equally by the Government of India and the RBI.
  • RBI divested its stake in NABARD and NHB in 2019, and both organisations are now fully owned by the GoI.
  • It is an apex regulatory body for the overall regulation of RRBs and cooperative banks in India. Section 35(6) of the Banking Regulation Act, of 1949, empowers NABARD to conduct an inspection of State Cooperative Banks (StCBs), Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), and District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs).

questions.question: The headquarters of SIDBI is located in _____.
questions.explanation:
• SIDBI is a statutory body and a principal development financial institution for financing, promotion, and development of the MSME sector in India.

  • It was set up in April of 1990, and its headquarters is situated in Lucknow.

  • The current Chairman & MD of SIDBI is Sivasubramanian Ramanan.

questions.question: Bankers Institute of Rural development (BIRD),  a training establishment for undertaking training,  research, and consultancy in the area of agriculture  and rural development banking was established by  _______.
questions.explanation:
• Bankers Institute of Rural development (BIRD), a training establishment of NABARD for undertaking training, research, and consultancy  in the area of agriculture and rural development banking was established in 1984 by NABARD.
  • The Institute is engaged in training and capacity building of the officials of the Rural Financial Institutions viz., Commercial Banks (CBs), Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), Cooperative Banks, and Government, and Non-Government organizations particularly in Eastern and North Eastern Regions.
  • BIRD Headquarters is  located in Lucknow

questions.question: National Housing Bank was established on the recommendation of which committee?
questions.explanation:
NHB was established as per the National Housing Bank Act 1987  and was established in 1988. It's Headquarter lies in Delhi. It was established after the recommendation of Rang Rajan Committee.

NHB is an apex regulatory body for overall regulation and licensing of housing finance companies in India. In 2019, Govt of India buys 100% stake at worth ₹ 1400 crore, from them NHB works under Govt of India but RBI is a regulator.

questions.question:
Which of the following roles does NHB perform?

  1. Regulating and supervising housing finance companies (HFCs)
  2. Providing financial assistance to housing finance institutions
  3. Acting as the principal agency to promote housing finance
  4. Directly constructing residential properties for public sale
  5. Ensuring the sound functioning of housing finance institutions
questions.explanation:
Correct answer is Only 1, 2, 3, & 5.

  • NHB is responsible for regulating and supervising housing finance companies (HFCs), providing financial assistance to housing finance institutions, and promoting housing finance across India.
  • However, NHB does not engage in the direct construction of residential properties for public sale.
  • Its role is more focused on the financial and regulatory aspects of housing finance rather than on real estate development.

questions.question: What is the Authorized Capital of ECGC Limited?
questions.explanation:
• ECGC Ltd. is the seventh largest credit insurer of the world in terms of coverage of national exports.
  • The present paid-up capital of the company is Rs. 2500 crores and authorized capital Rs. 5000 crores.

questions.question: Which of the following categories is not covered under Priority Sector Lending?

• Priority Sector means those sectors which the Government of India and Reserve Bank of India consider as important for the development of the basic needs of the country and are to be given priority over other sectors.

questions.question: When did Priority Sector Lending Certificates (PSL-Cs) were introduced?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'A' that is '2016'.
  • Priority Sector Lending Certificates (PSL-Cs) were introduced in 2016 to support comparative advantage of different banks in their respective areas of specialization.

Key Info: 

  • PSL-Cs are a mechanism that allows banks that exceed their Priority Sector Lending (PSL) targets to sell the excess to other banks that are falling short.
  • The certificates are traded on the RBI's electronic trading platform called e-Kuber.
  • There are four types of PSLCs: Agriculture, Small & Marginal Farmers, Micro Enterprises, and General.
  • The system is designed to enable a more efficient distribution of credit to priority sectors without transferring actual loan assets or risk.

questions.question: Who issues priority sector lending guidelines in India?
questions.explanation:
• In India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issues priority sector lending guidelines.
  • These guidelines are aimed at promoting economic development by providing loans to sectors such as agriculture, micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), and rural development at a lower interest rate.
  • The RBI reviews and updates these guidelines periodically to ensure that they remain effective in achieving the intended objectives.

questions.question: Priority Sector Lending guidelines are not applicable to which out of following type of banks?
questions.explanation:
• Priority Sector Lending (PSL) guidelines were introduced by the Reserve Bank of India to promote access to finance for underserved and disadvantaged sections of society including low-income households, small and medium enterprises, farmers, and non-resident Indians.
  • Though PSL norms are designed to encourage lending to these sectors, they do not apply to payments banks. Payments banks are financial institutions licensed by the Reserve Bank of India to provide basic banking services such as accepting deposits, making withdrawals, and issuing payments and remittance services.

questions.question: What is total priority sector target for Domestic scheduled commercial banks (excluding Regional Rural Banks and Small Finance Banks) as percentage of Adjusted Net Bank Credit or Credit Equivalent Amount of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure, whichever is higher?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'D' that is '40%'.
  • As per the RBI’s Priority Sector Lending (PSL) guidelines, Domestic Scheduled Commercial Banks (excluding RRBs and SFBs) are required to lend 40% of their Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) or Credit Equivalent Amount of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure (CEOBE), whichever is higher, to the priority sector.

Key Info: 

  • Priority Sector means those sectors which the Government of India and Reserve Bank of India consider as important for the development of the basic needs of the country and are to be given priority over other sectors.
  • The banks are mandated to encourage the growth of such sectors with adequate and timely credit.
  • Priority Sector Lending refers to those sectors of the economy which may not get timely and adequate credit in the absence of this special dispensation.
  • The targets and sub-targets for banks under priority sector are as follows:
  • For - Domestic scheduled commercial banks (excluding Regional Rural Banks and Small Finance Banks) and Foreign banks with 20 branches and above
  1. Total Priority Sector - 40 per cent of Adjusted Net Bank Credit or Credit Equivalent Amount of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure, whichever is higher.
  2. Agriculture sector - 18 per cent of ANBC or Credit Equivalent Amount of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure, whichever is higher.
  3. Micro Enterprises - 7.5 percent of ANBC or Credit Equivalent Amount of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure, whichever is higher.
  4. Advances to Weaker Sections - 10 percent of ANBC or Credit Equivalent Amount of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure, whichever is higher.
